On the phone to the Konzerthaus
It's December. Mara hasn't forgotten Mrs Hoffmann's wish: to play in a real concert hall one more time. She rings the Konzerthaus Berlin on Gendarmenmarkt.
Konzerthaus Berlin, Bauer speaking, good afternoon. How can I help you?
Good afternoon. My name is Mara Ionescu. I have a rather unusual question. Can you tell me who is in charge of programme planning?
It's about my neighbour. Her name is Margarete Hoffmann. I don't know whether the name means anything to you. She was a pianist in the sixties. She gave her first concert in 1956, at your hall.
Hoffmann… One moment. Yes! Margarete Hoffmann, the Chopin specialist. I have one of her records. Is she still alive?
Yes, she's ninety-one. And she plays every evening. I wanted to ask whether there might be any chance of her playing at your hall once more. Even briefly, in a small hall.
Hm. I can't tell you straight away whether that's possible. First I'd need to know how well she still plays and how long she can sit at the piano.
I understand. Can I send you a recording? I filmed her last summer, in the courtyard, with the window open.
Yes, please do. And tell me: does Mrs Hoffmann know you're calling me?
No. I'm not sure she'd want that. She always says she's too old. But in the autumn she said she'd love to play in front of an audience one more time.
Send me the video. I'll get back to you in two weeks. I can't promise anything. But I'm already wondering why we didn't think of this ourselves.

1. Indirect questions with a question word
A direct question can be “wrapped” inside a sentence: Ich weiß nicht…, Können Sie mir sagen…? The question word stays, and the conjugated verb goes to the END:
Können Sie mir sagen, wann das Konzert beginnt?
Ich weiß nicht, wo sie wohnt.
Ich frage mich, warum sie aufgehört hat.
Ich möchte wissen, wie lange sie spielen kann.
Indirect questions are more polite than direct ones. At a counter or on the phone, “Können Sie mir sagen, wo…?” sounds much better than “Wo ist…?”.
For questions with a yes / no answer (no question word), you use “ob” = whether, if:
Ich weiß nicht, ob sie morgen kommt.
Ich kann nicht sagen, ob das geht.
Sie hat gefragt, ob wir Zeit haben.
Ich bin nicht sicher, ob sie noch spielen kann.

“ob” ≠ “wenn”! Both can mean “if” in English. “ob” = question (I don't know IF / WHETHER she's coming). “wenn” = condition (IF she comes, we'll be happy). “Ich weiß nicht, wenn…” is wrong. Tip: if you can say “whether”, it's “ob”.
Watch the punctuation: if the main clause is a question (“Wissen Sie, …?”), you put a question mark at the end. If it's a statement (“Ich weiß nicht, …”), you put a full stop.

Mara sent the video that same evening. It was only three minutes long, a bit shaky, filmed on her phone in the courtyard during the party in February: the open window on the fourth floor, the fairy lights, the music flowing down into the little courtyard and, at the end, the applause from all the windows. Then she waited.

The two weeks were long. Every day Mara wondered whether she had made a mistake. What if Mr Bauer said no? What if he said yes and Mrs Hoffmann said no? What if she got angry because Mara had gone behind her back? She told only Ludwig.

It was a strange time in other ways too. Andrei had flown back to Sibiu after his week in Berlin, and Lena went about the bakery with a face that was happy and sad at the same time. Every evening at ten they talked on the phone, and every morning at four Andrei wrote a message: “Now you're kneading the dough.” Lena kept her phone next to the oven and answered with fingers covered in flour. Mara sometimes wondered whether love can last over one thousand two hundred kilometres. Then she saw Lena's face when her phone lit up at four and stopped wondering.

You're asking me whether Margarete will be angry? Of course she'll be angry. At first. She'll grumble and say she's too old, that her hands are too slow, that nobody wants to listen to an old woman. And then she'll practise all night.
On the fourteenth day Mara's phone rang while she was preparing medication in the nurses' room. A Berlin number. She went quickly out into the corridor.
Ms Ionescu? Bauer, from the Konzerthaus. I've seen the video. I showed it to my colleagues. And then I showed it to my mother, who had lessons with Mrs Hoffmann as a girl. She cried.

“My mother's name is Ilse,” Mr Bauer went on. “She was twelve when she came to Mrs Hoffmann, in 1963. She says Mrs Hoffmann was the strictest teacher in the world. But also the best. She taught her that you don't play with your fingers but with your breath. My mother couldn't become a pianist; she became a doctor. But she still plays every Sunday. When she saw the video, she immediately asked whether she could come to the concert. In the front row.”

He explained the plan to her. In March an event called “Generations” was taking place at the Konzerthaus: young music students playing together with older musicians who had once been famous. An evening in the Small Hall, with two hundred seats. Mrs Hoffmann could play at the end, two or three pieces, as many as she wanted. They would put a comfortable chair on the stage and organise a lift for her. There was only one condition.
She has to want it herself. I don't want us to push an elderly lady onto a stage. Ask her whether she feels like it. And then tell me what she said. Quite honestly.

On Wednesday, Mara's day on the fourth floor, she climbed the stairs with a pounding heart. She had a piece of Black Forest gateau from Lena with her, just in case. Mrs Hoffmann was sitting at the window, in the grey blanket Mara had given her for her birthday, looking down at the courtyard, where the first snow lay.
Mrs Hoffmann, I have to tell you something. And I don't know whether you'll be pleased or angry.

She told her everything. About the video, the phone call, Mr Bauer and his mother, the evening in March. Mrs Hoffmann listened without interrupting. Her face showed nothing. When Mara had finished, there was a long silence. Outside, the snow was falling softly on the chestnut tree.

Child, you don't know what you've done. I'm ninety-one. My fingers are stiff. Sometimes I forget what day it is. And you want me to play Chopin in front of two hundred people? I don't even know whether I can manage the steps up to the stage.
There's a lift. And I'd be next to you the whole time. But you don't have to. Mr Bauer said you should only do it if you really want to.

Mrs Hoffmann looked out of the window again. She looked at her hands, thin and full of spots, with long fingers. Then she got up, slowly, went to the piano and opened the lid. She didn't play anything. She just put her hands on the keys and left them there, motionless, as if she were asking them something.
Tell this Mr Bauer that I'll think about it. And tell him I'd like to know whether the piano in the Small Hall is still the old Steinway. I played on it in 1956. If they still have it… then maybe.

That evening at nine the whole building heard the piano on the fourth floor. But it wasn't the usual quiet piece. It was scales. Up and down, up and down, again and again, slowly at first, then faster, for a whole hour. Ludwig sat under his yellow lamp, listened and smiled. Then he wrote Mara a message, slowly, with one finger: “SHE'S PRACTISING. TOLD YOU. LUDWIG.”
Mara read the message in bed and laughed. Then she wrote Mr Bauer a short email: “She's thinking about it. And she's already practising. I think that means yes.”
